title: A Very Irregular Education
subtitle: How Theodore Roosevelt Was Schooled
intro: He never sat in a classroom until he was seventeen, was hopeless at Latin and unbeatable at natural history, worked drearily through an essay on the Gracchi, and walked out of law school after a year. Thirteen questions for the start of term.
heroAlt: Holworthy Hall in Harvard Yard, photographed in the nineteenth century
heroCredit: Holworthy Hall, Harvard Yard. Photograph by William Notman & Son. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

badge.title: A Very Irregular Education
badge.shareText: I scored {score}/{total} on the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library's quiz about T.R.'s schooling — {tier}. Try it:

tiers.name: Strong in Some Subjects
tiers.line: Weak in others, like the boy himself.

tiers.name: Dragged Through the Gracchi
tiers.line: By main strength. He knew the feeling.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt never spent a day in an ordinary school before college. By his own account, why not?
options: Ahead in some subjects, far behind in others
The family travelled abroad too much for it
No school in New York would take an asthmatic boy
questions.explanation: "I could not go to school because I knew so much less than most boys of my age in some subjects and so much more in others," he wrote. Illness had kept him home and long family journeys had kept him abroad, and the result was a boy who could hold a serious conversation about bird taxonomy and could not construe a page of Livy. His aunt Anna had taught the children their lessons at home; after that came tutors.
questions.imageAlt: Tintype of the four Roosevelt children
questions.credit: Roosevelt children, tintype. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which subjects did Roosevelt call himself lamentably weak in?
questions.explanation: His own word, lamentably. The strong side of the ledger was science, history, geography, and unexpected patches of German and French. Two years of hard drilling by a young Harvard graduate named Arthur Cutler closed the gap enough to get him through the entrance examinations, and Cutler is one of only two teachers Roosevelt bothers to thank by name in his memoirs.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt photographed as a college student
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college," 1876. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In the summer of 1873 the three younger Roosevelt children were left with a family in Dresden. What for?
questions.explanation: They boarded with the Minckwitz family, in the hope, as Roosevelt put it, that they would acquire some knowledge of the German language and literature. He came away with the language and a lasting passion for the Nibelungenlied, and repaid his hosts by filling the flat with hedgehogs and small reptiles that kept escaping from half-closed bureau drawers. The two Minckwitz sons were duelling-corps students from Leipzig; one had had the tip of his nose sliced off and sewn back on, and went by Sir Rhinoceros.
questions.imageAlt: The Roosevelt children and their cousins photographed in Dresden
questions.credit: Dresden Literary American Club. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt loaded his Harvard course list with two fields. Which?
questions.explanation: Where the elective system let him choose, he chose natural history and languages — German, Italian, French, Latin and Greek. In his sophomore year he took elementary botany and the comparative anatomy and physiology of vertebrates, the second of them taught by William James, alongside two courses of German and one of French. He had gone up to Cambridge meaning to be a working field naturalist, and he chose accordingly.
questions.imageAlt: Nineteenth-century view over Harvard Yard and Cambridge
questions.credit: Southern view from Memorial Hall, Harvard Yard. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt names one Harvard professor in his Autobiography as a man he owed a great deal to. What did he teach?
questions.explanation: A. S. Hill, the professor of English. Roosevelt thought he ought to have got far more out of writing his themes and forensics than he did, and put the failure down to his own lack of interest in the topics he was set. He saw almost nothing of President Eliot and very little of the rest of the faculty. Out of four years at Harvard, the two teachers who mattered to him were a private tutor and a professor of composition.
questions.imageAlt: The board of the Harvard Advocate in 1880, with Roosevelt among them
questions.credit: Harvard Advocate board, 1880. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: One Harvard assignment defeated Roosevelt completely. What was its subject?
questions.explanation: He was not, he admitted later, sufficiently developed to take an intelligent interest in the Gracchi. "I worked drearily at the Gracchi because I had to; my conscientious and much-to-be-pitied professor dragging me through the theme by main strength, with my feet firmly planted in dull and totally idea-proof resistance." In the same term, for no marks at all, he was drafting the opening chapters of a technical history of the naval war of 1812.
questions.credit: Holworthy Hall, Harvard Yard. Photograph by William Notman & Son. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt describe his own standing in his Harvard class?
options: He never troubled to find out
questions.explanation: That is his own phrase, and he immediately hedged it: he was not sure whether he meant a tenth of the men who entered or a tenth of those who graduated. Modern accounts give the size of that class two different ways, so his hedge is still the safest description available. He was given a Phi Beta Kappa key and disposed of it in half a sentence.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a Harvard undergraduate
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college," 1876. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt's senior thesis at Harvard argue for?
questions.explanation: "The Practicability of Equalizing Men and Women Before the Law." He wanted equal rights of inheritance, the vote, and admission to law school, and thought a woman should be free to keep her own name on marrying. He was twenty-one, and he started writing it two months after Alice Lee agreed to marry him — a coincidence of timing that his biographers have not been able to resist.
questions.credit: Harvard Advocate board, 1880. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt never took part in one common college activity, and spent a page of his memoirs defending that. What was it?
options: Rowing on the Charles for the college crew
questions.explanation: He had, he wrote, "not the slightest sympathy with debating contests in which each side is arbitrarily assigned a given proposition and told to maintain it without the least reference to whether those maintaining it believe in it or not." Colleges ought to turn out "young men with ardent convictions on the side of the right; not young men who can make a good argument for either right or wrong as their interest bids them." He did regret never studying elocution, which he was careful to treat as a separate complaint.
questions.imageAlt: View across Harvard Yard in the nineteenth century
questions.credit: Southern view from Memorial Hall, Harvard Yard. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt began studying law in the autumn of 1880. At which law school?
questions.explanation: Columbia Law School, then down in lower Manhattan on Great Jones Street. He walked to it from the family house on West 57th Street with Blackstone's Commentaries under his arm, read law in his uncle Robert's office as well, and lasted a year. Cross-examined in a New York courtroom thirty-five years later, he described himself with some precision as a man who had studied a year at Columbia and had never been admitted to the bar.
questions.imageAlt: The library of the Roosevelt house at 6 West 57th Street, New York
questions.credit: Library, 6 West 57th Street, New York. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which idea in the law repelled Roosevelt most?
options: The rule against perpetuities in land
questions.explanation: "The caveat emptor side of the law, like the caveat emptor side of business, seemed to me repellent; it did not make for social fair dealing." Let the buyer beware, he thought, came down in practice to the seller profiting at the buyer's expense rather than by a bargain good for both. He kept springing to his feet in Professor Dwight's lecture room to say so. Writing it up decades later he was fair to himself: "I was young; there was much in the judgment which I then formed on this matter which I should now revise."
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt seated with a book
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, seated portrait. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's legal studies stopped after a single year. What was he doing instead by the end of 1881?
options: Running a ranch in Dakota Territory
Sitting in the New York State Assembly
Reporting for a New York newspaper
questions.explanation: He was elected to the Assembly in November 1881, at twenty-three, and never went back to Columbia. He had joined his local Republican district association almost as soon as he left Harvard, and the men he had grown up among told him politics were low and better left to saloon-keepers and horsecar conductors. He decided that was an argument for going rather than staying away.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a young man
questions.credit: "Theo. Roosevelt at college," 1876. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Looking back, what did Roosevelt say Harvard had actually done for him?
options: Nothing at all — he called it four wasted years
Good in general, little in the studies
questions.explanation: "I thoroughly enjoyed Harvard, and I am sure it did me good, but only in the general effect, for there was very little in my actual studies which helped me in after life." What he credited was people, not curriculum — a tutor and a professor of English. What he wanted colleges to produce was young men with convictions rather than young men who could argue anything. It is a hard verdict from a man who left with a Phi Beta Kappa key and went on writing books for the next forty years.
questions.credit: Holworthy Hall, Harvard Yard. Photograph by William Notman & Son. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
